abstract: Confocal laser scanning fluorescence microscopy (CLSFM) is widely used for three-dimensional live-cell imaging. However, high irradiance is required to overcome dark counts in photodetectors, often leading to observation bias. In this study, we examine whether a CLSFM system equipped with a virtually dark-count-free superconducting transition-edge sensor (TES) can enable live-cell imaging under low irradiance, thereby mitigating observation bias. Using green fluorescent protein-tagged HeLa cells, we determined the minimum laser power required for live-cell imaging and demonstrated suppression of photobleaching and cell-division arrest during long-term observation. Innate fluorescence signature analysis revealed that TES-CLSFM could discriminate between two oleaginous yeast species with different lipid productivities at ca. 1/400 the irradiance required by conventional CLSFM. These results establish TES-CLSFM as a minimally invasive imaging modality for the quantitative physiological assessment of living cells.
